--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Work Breakdown Structures (WBS) ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Explain** what a WBS is and how it links scope, schedule, and budget. 2. **Decompose** a project into deliverables, work packages, and activities. 3. **Apply** the 100 % rule, the mutually-exclusive rule, and "plan outcomes, not actions." 4. **Choose** an appropriate level of decomposition using the 8/80 and single-reporting-period rules of thumb. 5. **Number** a WBS and write a WBS dictionary entry for a work package. 6. **Roll up** cost and effort from work packages to the total project. 7. **State** the six requirements of a valid project contract and the purpose of work authorization.
Before we begin: how do you eat an elephant? One bite at a time. *"Project managers cannot manage projects. Project managers manage pieces of projects."* The WBS is how you cut the elephant into bites.
## Introduction: from a scope statement to something you can manage You have a signed scope statement for the RC-vehicle replica. It is still far too big to schedule, budget, or assign. The **work breakdown structure** is the bridge: it takes the total scope and breaks it into **deliverables**, then **work packages**, then **activities** small enough that one person can own each one and you can put a real number on it. > **Definition.** A WBS is a **deliverable-oriented** grouping of project > components that organizes and defines the **total scope** of the project. A well-built WBS lets the team **plan every step**, **collect and organize** the information each task needs, and **assign** manageable chunks to team members. It also enables the **WBS dictionary**, which pins down the requirements for each task. ::: {.callout-note} **Industry snapshot.** An automotive program WBS separates *body*, *powertrain integration*, *electrical*, *validation*, and *launch* --- each a deliverable, not an action. A food-plant install WBS breaks out *utilities*, *process equipment*, *controls*, *sanitation qualification*, and *commissioning*. A defense contract WBS follows a mandated standard (MIL-STD-881) so the customer can track cost against the exact same structure the contractor uses. :::
## The hierarchy ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: The `label.size` argument of `geom_label()` is deprecated as of ggplot2 3.5.0. ℹ Please use the `linewidth` argument instead. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A partial WBS for the RC-vehicle project. Level 1 is the project; Level 2 the major deliverables; Level 3 the work packages. Numbering encodes the hierarchy.](05-Work-Breakdown-Structures_files/figure-html/fig-wbs-tree-05-1.png){#fig-wbs-tree-05 fig-align='center' width=1248} ::: ::: - **Level 1** --- the project. *What is the project?* - **Level 2** --- the summary level: the project's major deliverables. - **Level 3** --- the start of the **work package** level (more levels if the package is complex). The same content can be shown as a **tree** (good for communicating structure) or a **tabular / indented list** (good for working). Both carry the numbering. ## Design principles ### The 100 % rule The WBS includes **100 % of the work** in the scope --- all deliverables, internal, external, and interim --- and **no more**. At every level, the **sum of the children equals the parent**, and nothing outside the scope appears. ### Worked Example 1: does this WBS roll up to 100 %? The "1.1 Body & Frame" deliverable is estimated at **340 hours**. Its four work packages are estimated at 120, 90, 70, and 60 hours. Live cell --- change the parent estimate or the work-package hours and watch the 100 % check. ```{=html}

WBS 100% Rule Check

h
h

```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: wbs-rollup-example-05 parent_hours <- 340 h_outer <- 120 # 1.1.1 Outer body design h_inner <- 90 # 1.1.2 Inner frame design h_select <- 70 # 1.1.3 Material selection h_review <- 60 # 1.1.4 Design review & release children_hours <- c("1.1.1 Outer body design" = h_outer, "1.1.2 Inner frame design" = h_inner, "1.1.3 Material selection" = h_select, "1.1.4 Design review & release" = h_review) child_sum <- sum(children_hours) # Chart: the four children stacked beside the parent estimate stack <- rbind(cbind(children_hours, 0), c(0, parent_hours)) colnames(stack) <- c("Children", "Parent") par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) barplot(stack, col = c("#2980b9", "#16a085", "#8e44ad", "#e67e22", "#34495e"), ylim = c(0, max(child_sum, parent_hours) * 1.1), ylab = "Hours", main = "Do the children add up to the parent?") abline(h = parent_hours, lty = 2, lwd = 3, col = "#e74c3c") if (child_sum == parent_hours) { cat("OK: the children account for exactly 100% of the parent\n") } else if (child_sum < parent_hours) { cat(sprintf("!!GAP: %g h of the parent's scope is in no work package!!\n", parent_hours - child_sum)) } else { cat(sprintf("!!OVER: the children exceed the parent by %g h (scope crept in)!!\n", child_sum - parent_hours)) } cat(sprintf("Sum of children %g h\n", child_sum)) cat(sprintf("Parent estimate %g h\n", parent_hours)) cat(sprintf("Children as share of parent %.1f%%\n", 100 * child_sum / parent_hours)) ```
Here the children sum to 340 --- the deliverable is fully decomposed with nothing missing and nothing extra. ### Mutually exclusive **No overlap** between WBS elements. Overlap causes duplicated work, confusion over who is responsible, and messy cost accounting. If element names are ambiguous, the **WBS dictionary** disambiguates them. ### Plan outcomes, not actions Define elements as **results** ("Training module completed"), not **actions** ("write script", "record video", "upload"). Action lists always capture too many or too few steps --- breaking the 100 % rule --- and they over-prescribe *how* the work is done, killing the team's ingenuity. ### Try it yourself: outcome or action? ```{=html}
``` ### Try it yourself: does it roll up to 100 %? ```{=html}
``` ## Level of detail A work package at the **activity level** is a task that: - can be **realistically and confidently estimated**; - makes no practical sense to break down further; - produces a **measurable deliverable**; and - forms a unique package that **could be outsourced or contracted out**. **Rules of thumb for how far to decompose:** - **80-hour rule** --- no work package (single deliverable at the lowest level) exceeds ~80 hours of effort. - **One reporting period** --- no package is longer than a single progress-reporting period (if you report monthly, nothing runs longer than a month). - **8-hour floor** --- generally do not define a task below ~8 hours; below that you are micromanaging. - **"If it makes sense"** --- apply common sense. ### Try it yourself: decomposition check ```{webr-r} #| label: wbs-decomp-05 packages <- data.frame( id = c("1.1.1", "1.2.1", "1.3.1", "1.3.4", "1.4.2"), name = c("Outer body design", "Motor/controller procurement", "Prototype assembly", "Tighten one fastener", "Full regulatory approval campaign"), hours = c(64, 40, 72, 1.5, 260) ) flag <- ifelse(packages$hours > 80, "TOO BIG (> 80 h -- split it)", ifelse(packages$hours < 8, "TOO SMALL (< 8 h -- roll it up)", "ok")) out <- cbind(packages, verdict = flag) print(out, row.names = FALSE) cat(sprintf("\n%d of %d packages need re-sizing.\n", sum(flag != "ok"), nrow(packages))) ``` ### Try it yourself: does it fit inside one reporting period? The 8/80 rule checks **effort hours**; the one-reporting-period rule checks **calendar span** against how often you report --- a different failure mode. A package can be well under 80 hours and still run longer than your reporting cycle if it is thin, spread-out work. Live cell --- change the reporting cadence or a package's span and see which packages need to be split or tracked by percent-complete instead. ```{=html}

Reporting-Cycle Check

```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: wbs-reporting-period-05 reporting_cycle_days <- 14 # biweekly status reports span_concept <- 10 # 1.1.1 Concept CAD span_motor <- 25 # 1.2.1 Motor/controller procurement span_drop <- 5 # 1.5.1 Drop/durability test span_cert <- 12 # 1.5.2 Toy-safety certification packages <- data.frame( id = c("1.1.1", "1.2.1", "1.5.1", "1.5.2"), name = c("Concept CAD", "Motor/controller procurement", "Drop/durability test", "Toy-safety certification"), span_days = c(span_concept, span_motor, span_drop, span_cert) ) packages$too_long <- packages$span_days > reporting_cycle_days n_bad <- sum(packages$too_long) par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) barplot(packages$span_days, names.arg = packages$id, col = ifelse(packages$too_long, "#e74c3c", "#16a085"), ylim = c(0, max(packages$span_days, reporting_cycle_days) * 1.15), ylab = "Span (days)", main = "Work-package span vs. reporting cycle") abline(h = reporting_cycle_days, lty = 2, lwd = 3, col = "#2c3e50") if (n_bad > 0) { cat(sprintf("!!%d of %d packages need attention!!\n", n_bad, nrow(packages))) } else { cat(sprintf("All %d packages fit within one reporting cycle\n", nrow(packages))) } cat(sprintf("Reporting cadence every %d days\n", reporting_cycle_days)) for (i in seq_len(nrow(packages))) { verdict <- if (packages$too_long[i]) { sprintf("!!%g days: split or report %% complete!!", packages$span_days[i]) } else { sprintf("%g days: fits within one cycle", packages$span_days[i]) } cat(sprintf("%s %s %s\n", packages$id[i], packages$name[i], verdict)) } ```
### Try it yourself: is the package the right size? ```{=html}
``` ## Why the WBS matters ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The WBS feeds four downstream planning activities. Get it wrong and the estimate, the schedule, the staffing plan, and the risk register are all built on sand.](05-Work-Breakdown-Structures_files/figure-html/fig-wbs-hub-05-1.png){#fig-wbs-hub-05 fig-align='center' width=864} ::: ::: ## The WBS dictionary The dictionary is used to **control what work is done and when**, **prevent scope creep**, and **capture the effort** for each task. Physically, teams post the work packages on a wall in logical work-flow order; **removing them in numerical order generates the dictionary**. Each entry --- a **task description** --- records: - Task description (what work is authorized) - Quantified objectives and deliverables (cross-referenced to the charter) - Product description; acceptance criteria (how the owner checks their own work) - Assumptions; resources assigned; duration; cost; due date - Interdependencies (before this task / after this task) - Project manager approval and date ## Work authorization and contracts Once the scope is decomposed into work packages, stakeholders formally agree on project content --- the **work authorization**. If the client is external, this includes the **contract sign-off**. A valid project-management contract requires all six of: 1. The legal **right** to contract 2. Legal **age** (18 in Ontario and Quebec; 19 or 21 elsewhere in Canada) 3. **Sound mind** at signing 4. Valid, legal **consideration** for both parties 5. A **legal scope of work** 6. **Offer and acceptance** Contracts also commonly contain: excusable delays; allowable costs; **liquidated damages** (non-performance / penalty clauses); inspection criteria; responsibility for correcting defects; and dispute-resolution mechanisms. ### Try it yourself: cost roll-up from the WBS ```{webr-r} #| label: wbs-cost-rollup-05 # Work-package costs (direct), grouped by Level-2 deliverable. wp <- data.frame( deliverable = c(rep("1.1 Body & Frame", 3), rep("1.2 Drive & Controls", 2), rep("1.3 Assembly & Test", 3), rep("1.4 Launch", 2)), package = c("Outer body", "Inner frame", "Material selection", "Motor/controller", "Wiring harness", "Prototype assembly", "Drop test", "EMC test", "Packaging design", "Approvals"), cost = c(18000, 14000, 6000, 140000, 9000, 21000, 12000, 15000, 8000, 6000) ) by_deliverable <- tapply(wp$cost, wp$deliverable, sum) cat("Roll-up to Level 2:\n") for (d in names(by_deliverable)) cat(sprintf(" %-22s $%s\n", d, format(by_deliverable[d], big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("\nLevel 1 (total project direct cost): $%s\n", format(sum(wp$cost), big.mark = " "))) cat("\nThis roll-up only works because the WBS obeys the 100% and\n") cat("mutually-exclusive rules -- every dollar is counted once, and all of them.\n") ``` ### Try it yourself: roll the hours up the tree The leaf work packages carry their hours. Work up the tree: each deliverable is the sum of its packages, and the project is the sum of the deliverables. Each team picks its own **data set**. ::: {.column-body-outset} ```{=html}
``` :::
Show the worked solution For data set 1: 1.1 = 60 + 35 + 70 = 165 h; 1.2 = 80 + 95 = 175 h; 1.3 = 50 + 30 = 80 h; the project is 165 + 175 + 80 = **420 h**. The electronics branch is 175 / 420 = 42 % of the work. The roll-up only works because every hour is in exactly one package: the 100 % rule and mutual exclusivity.
## Key Takeaways - A **WBS** is a **deliverable-oriented** decomposition of the **total scope** into deliverables → work packages → activities. PMs manage the pieces. - **Numbering** encodes the hierarchy: Level 1 project, Level 2 deliverables, Level 3+ work packages. - Obey the three design rules: **100 % rule** (children sum to the parent, never more), **mutually exclusive** (no overlap), and **plan outcomes, not actions**. - Size work packages with the **8/80 rule** and the **one-reporting-period** rule; below ~8 h you are micromanaging, above ~80 h you cannot estimate confidently. - The WBS feeds **estimating, scheduling, staffing, and risk** --- errors propagate to all four. - The **WBS dictionary** locks down each task's description, acceptance criteria, resources, and interdependencies, and helps prevent scope creep. - **Work authorization** formalizes agreement on content; a valid contract needs all **six** legal elements and usually carries **liquidated-damages** and dispute clauses. ## Case Study: Meridian R/C — Week 5 ::: {.callout-tip .case-study title="📁 CASE STUDY FILE — Week 5: Cutting the Trailblazer Into Bites"} You're three weeks into the Meridian Trailblazer prototype, and Daniel Cho's $800,000 charter ceiling is signed. It's time to stop describing the project and start decomposing it. This week you sat down with Priya Nandakumar (tooling), Marcus Webb (procurement), and Sofia Reyes (quality and test) to turn "build a prototype that passes Kestrel Retail Group's durability testing and toy-safety certification" into a WBS the team can actually schedule, budget, and staff. You started at Level 1 with **1.0 Meridian Trailblazer Prototype** and split it into seven Level-2 deliverables, each owned by a named function so nobody can later claim a piece of scope belongs to someone else: - **1.1 Design & Engineering** — 1.1.1 Concept CAD, 1.1.2 Detailed design release - **1.2 Tooling & Fabrication** — 1.2.1 Body tooling, 1.2.2 Frame tooling - **1.3 Motor & Controls Integration** - **1.4 Prototype Assembly** - **1.5 Testing & Certification** — 1.5.1 Drop/durability test, 1.5.2 Toy-safety certification - **1.6 Packaging & Client Sample Shipment** - **1.7 Project Management** (cross-cutting) Notice what this structure is *not*. It is not "call the tooling vendor" or "email Sofia the test plan" — every element names a deliverable or result (a released design, a qualified tool, an integrated drive system, a certified sample) rather than an action, exactly as the outcomes-not-actions rule demands. Priya pushed back once, wanting to fold "1.2 Tooling & Fabrication" and "1.3 Motor & Controls Integration" into one bucket since her team touches both — but that would blur ownership between tooling (hers) and the MCS/Paragon procurement decision (Marcus's), so you kept them mutually exclusive instead. You also ran the 100% rule on 1.2: body tooling (1.2.1) and frame tooling (1.2.2) are the *only* children of Tooling & Fabrication — nothing about motor sourcing or assembly labour is allowed to hide inside that branch, and nothing about tooling is allowed to leak into 1.3 or 1.4. And you sized 1.7 Project Management as its own Level-2 element specifically so PM effort never gets smuggled into a technical deliverable's hours — the same mistake you'll later coach a student through in the practice problems. Sofia flagged that 1.5's two children stay far enough apart in scope — durability is physical stress testing, certification is regulatory sign-off — that a failure in one doesn't get miscoded as a failure in the other when Kestrel's 100,000-unit decision comes down to those two checkboxes. ::: ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Fix the 100 % rule violation The "1.3 Assembly & Test" deliverable is estimated at 300 h. Its packages are listed as: Prototype assembly (110 h), Drop test (60 h), EMC test (70 h), Prototype assembly rework (40 h), Write the test report (30 h), *and* "General project management (50 h)." What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
Solution The children sum to 360 h --- 60 h **over** 100 % of the parent. Two problems: "Prototype assembly rework" overlaps "Prototype assembly" (not mutually exclusive --- fold rework into the assembly package or make it a contingency), and "General project management" is **not part of this deliverable's scope** --- PM effort belongs in its own Level-2 element (e.g. "1.0.1 Project Management"), not smuggled into a technical deliverable.
Problem 2: Outcome or action? Rewrite these action-style entries as outcome-style WBS elements: 1. "Call three carbon-fibre suppliers and get quotes" 2. "Run the mould 20 times and measure the parts" 3. "Email the drawings to the customer for approval"
Model answers 1. "Carbon-fibre supplier selected and quoted." 2. "Moulding process capability established." 3. "Customer design approval obtained." Each is a result you can mark done or not done, and it does not dictate the method.
Problem 3 (discussion): how deep should the RC-vehicle WBS go? Your draft WBS has a work package "Design the outer body" estimated at 180 h and spanning 6 weeks, and another, "Deburr the frame jig", estimated at 2 h. Using the rules of thumb, what do you do with each?
Discussion points "Design the outer body" breaks both the 80-hour rule and (if you report every 2 weeks) the single-reporting-period rule --- split it into concept, detailed CAD, and design-release packages. "Deburr the frame jig" is below the 8-hour floor --- roll it into the jig-fabrication package rather than tracking it as its own line.
